passage: When Tenzin was two, his mother Dolma came home after a bad day and stood over him in the hallway, shoulders high, jaw tight, saying "Shoes, please" in a flat voice. Tenzin dropped his toy and backed under the table. The next evening Dolma crouched down to his height, hands loose on her knees, and said the very same words. Tenzin toddled straight into her arms. At ten, he sank low in his chair during a long fractions lesson, chin on his fist, turning the problem over in his head. The teacher paused at his desk. "Sit up, please. I want to see you're with us." He straightened, cheeks hot, though he had been further along than half the class. At twenty, in the canteen, he told his friend Nikita about a trek he wanted to plan. She leaned back with her arms folded, gazing at the ceiling. His voice slowed. Then he asked, "You've gone quiet. Is it the trip, or is your head still sore from the lab?" Nikita groaned. "Head. Keep going 🙂"

qa.q: Where did Tenzin tell Nikita about the trek he wanted to plan?
qa.a: He told her in the canteen.

qa.q: How did Tenzin's understanding of a person's body differ at two, at ten and at twenty?
qa.a: At two he backed under the table when Dolma stood over him stiff, and came to her when she crouched; at ten the teacher read his slouch as not being with them; at twenty he asked Nikita about her leaning back instead of guessing. A body is a clue, and only the older Tenzin checks it with a question.

qa.q: What was Tenzin probably feeling when the teacher told him to sit up?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a little unfairly judged, shown by his hot cheeks after being one of the students furthest along.

qa.q: What could Tenzin's teacher try next time when a student slouches?
qa.a: They could ask quietly whether the student is tired or thinking, and look at the student's work before deciding they are bored.

grounding: One boy's reading of body posture across three ages: from reacting to a parent's stance, to being misjudged for slouching, to checking a friend's leaning back with a question.

passage: Chaitanya's end-of-term exam was three weeks away, so instead of one long night of reading, he and his study partner Uma made a plan: forty minutes a day, a different chapter each time. Every session began with a blank page. Chaitanya wrote down everything he could remember about the last chapter, then checked. "It's so much slower than rereading," he said, wincing at the gaps. Uma shrugged. "That's the gap we're fixing." Three days later they revisited the same chapter just as it had gone hazy, and the answers came back with a tug of effort. He passed with room to spare. Four years on, Chaitanya was working at a logistics firm. His new colleague Naveen watched him open a notebook before a client call. "Forgot the export steps again?" Naveen asked. Chaitanya nodded without embarrassment. "I only use them twice a year. I keep the steps here, and every few weeks I run through the important ones from memory." He tapped the notebook. "The rest can fade. My head has to make room for something." Naveen grinned and pulled out his own list.

qa.q: How long was Chaitanya and Uma's daily study session?
qa.a: Their session was forty minutes a day, with a different chapter each time.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya's way of dealing with forgetting change between his exam term and his working years?
qa.a: As a student he went back to the chapter just as it had gone hazy and wrote down what he could remember; at work he keeps the steps in a notebook and runs through the important ones from memory every few weeks, letting the rest fade.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he opened his notebook in front of Naveen?
qa.a: He felt at ease, not ashamed; he nodded without embarrassment and explained his system.

qa.q: What small step would help Naveen after seeing Chaitanya's notebook?
qa.a: He could write his own list of rarely used steps and set a regular time to run through the important ones from memory. 🙂

grounding: The same person handles forgetting first by spacing and self-testing as a student, then by notes and interval reviews as a working adult who accepts fading as normal.

passage: Yusuf was nine when the blinking started, and a small sniff that came in bursts. In class he felt a tight urge build behind his nose until the sniff escaped, and a boy behind him whispered, "Stop it." Yusuf's face burned and the sniffs came faster. At home his mother Vandana simply kept peeling oranges and said, "Come and help me, dear." While he pressed the fruit apart, the sniffing faded. At fifteen, Yusuf held everything in through the school day. His jaw ached by the last bell. He walked past the gate with his shoulders up, and only once his bedroom door was shut did the blinking and noises rush out. Afterwards he lay flat, worn out. His classmate Charu once caught him rubbing his eyes in the corridor and only said, "Want to walk to the library? It's quiet." Vandana knocked that evening with tea. "Nobody here minds. And if it ever gets in your way, we can ask the doctor what might help." He nodded, and for a long while nobody spoke.

qa.q: What did Vandana do when Yusuf's sniffing began at home?
qa.a: She kept peeling oranges and asked him to come and help her.

qa.q: What changed between Yusuf's tics at nine and at fifteen, and what stayed the same?
qa.a: At nine they burst out in class and shame made them worse, while at fifteen he held them in at school and released them at home, exhausted. In both years, calm company helped and blame did not.

qa.q: How was Yusuf feeling as he walked out past the school gate at fifteen?
qa.a: He felt tense and self-conscious, tired from holding everything in; his raised shoulders and aching jaw show it.

qa.q: How could Charu keep supporting Yusuf at school?
qa.a: She could keep offering quiet places to walk or sit, without staring, commenting or asking him to stop.

grounding: One child's tics across two ages: urges that shame makes worse at nine, then hidden effort at school and release at home at fifteen, eased by calm acceptance.

passage: At five, Nikita watched her friend Hafsa trip on the playground and scrape her knee. Nikita's mouth opened, tears streamed, and her feet would not move. Another child fetched the teacher, and Nikita cried harder at the sight of the knee. She cared very much; she simply could not get to Hafsa. At fifteen, Hafsa's grandmother died. Nikita listened for hours and cried with her, lay awake replaying it, and by the second week had started leaving messages unanswered. Hafsa's name on the screen made Nikita's chest tighten. She told her aunt, "I can't keep carrying it, and I feel like a bad friend." Her aunt sat with her and said the tiredness was real, and they planned one short visit that weekend. At twenty, Nikita was in her second year of nursing. She stood at a ward bedside after a hard shift, feeling nothing. She snapped at a classmate and wondered whether she had stopped caring. Her mentor Yogesh, who ran the practice sessions, listened. "You've been feeling for everyone all week," he said. "Rest and talk it through with me first."

qa.q: Who fetched the teacher when Hafsa scraped her knee?
qa.a: Another child fetched the teacher.

qa.q: How did Nikita's overwhelming feeling for others show up at five, at fifteen and at twenty?
qa.a: At five she cried and her feet would not move, so Hafsa got no help; at fifteen she cried with Hafsa, lay awake and left messages unanswered; at twenty she felt nothing at the bedside after a hard shift. Each time she cared very much, but the feeling swamped or drained her.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she stood at the bedside feeling nothing?
qa.a: She felt drained and worried that she no longer cared, which shows in her snapping and questioning herself.

qa.q: What could Nikita try so that she can keep caring for patients without wearing out?
qa.a: She could talk through hard shifts with Yogesh, rest properly, and take her feelings to someone she trusts rather than carrying them alone.

grounding: The same person's feeling-with overwhelms her at three ages, at five freezing, at fifteen withdrawing and at twenty going numb, each time exhaustion rather than lack of care.

passage: At nine, Sahil only ever did the sliding puzzle he had already solved. Jasleen, the librarian, slid a new one across the table. "Try this if you like." He pushed it back. "I'll get it wrong." Then he did his old puzzle a fifth time, quickly. At fifteen, he lost a debate final, and on the walk home he kept hearing the judges. His teammate Hafsa messaged about the next round. He typed "busy" and put the phone face down, thinking that everyone now knew he was not as clever as he had seemed. At twenty, Sahil filled in his course choices at the kitchen table. He loved drawing buildings, and the architecture stream had a long, uncertain admission process. Beside it sat an easy business elective with a nearly sure top grade. He read the two names again, the pencil hovering. Then he ticked the elective, closed the laptop, and told himself he would draw for fun on weekends. His sketchbook stayed at the bottom of his bag, unopened for months.

qa.q: Which puzzle did Sahil keep doing at the library?
qa.a: He kept doing the sliding puzzle he had already solved.

qa.q: How did Sahil's fear of getting things wrong shape what he did at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At nine it kept him to old puzzles, at fifteen it made him avoid the next debate because the loss felt like a verdict on him, and at twenty it steered him to an easy elective over the subject he loved. Each time, safety cost him a chance to learn or grow.

qa.q: What was Sahil thinking when he typed "busy" to Hafsa?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, believing the loss showed he was not as clever as people thought, so he wanted to hide from the next contest.

qa.q: What small step could help Sahil begin drawing buildings again?
qa.a: He could sketch a little each week and ask the architecture department how their admission process works, so a small try replaces the all-or-nothing choice.

grounding: One person's fear of failure moves from avoiding unfamiliar puzzles, to shame that stops him entering the next debate, to a safe course choice that shelves what he loves.

passage: At two, Wasim lined up his toy cars along the window ledge every morning and cried hard when the route to the nursery changed. He seldom looked up when his name was called, but at bedtime he pressed his forehead against his mother's arm and kept it there. She wrote her observations in a notebook to show the paediatrician. At fifteen, Wasim spent lunch breaks practising phrases and copying how his friend Yash raised his eyebrows and laughed. By evening he came home and dropped his bag, and sometimes could not answer anyone. His family left the lights low and did not ask questions. Twenty-five now, Wasim worked at a software firm. The open-plan floor made his head ring, and vague requests like "just sort it out" left him stuck. His manager Varun agreed to written tasks and let Wasim wear headphones. "Thank you," Wasim said afterwards. "I finally know what I'm meant to do by Friday." Varun nodded, and Wasim opened his laptop, shoulders down.

qa.q: What did Wasim line up on the window ledge every morning?
qa.a: He lined up his toy cars.

qa.q: How did Wasim's day-to-day experience change from toddlerhood to fifteen to twenty-five?
qa.a: At two he showed his love and distress in his own ways, at fifteen he hid his natural ways to fit in and then collapsed at home, and at twenty-five he could ask for written tasks and headphones. What changed most was that he was understood and able to rest or adjust.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when Varun agreed to written tasks?
qa.a: He felt relieved and grateful, since he now knew what was expected and his shoulders dropped.

qa.q: How could Wasim's family help after a day of masking at school?
qa.a: They can keep offering quiet, low-light time after school without questions, so he has a place where he does not need to hide his natural ways.

grounding: One person's autistic experience over time: distinctive ways of relating at two, masking followed by exhaustion at fifteen, and clear tasks and adjustments at work at twenty-five.
